transcript: So Ethan Slater wrote a play, but is it any good? Slater is the star and co-writer of this new play about the legendary mime, Marcel Marceau, who helped smuggle Jewish orphans out of France during WW2. The majority of the play takes place on a train, but we also flash forward to these children's futures as they remember this pivotal day with Marcel that saved their lives. The story feels a little bit like a spiritual successor to Roberto Benigni’s iconic film, Life is Beautiful, as it focuses on Marcel trying to use his comedic sensibilities to keep the children entertained and optimistic throughout this ordeal. But unlike in Life is Beautiful, these are not small children. These are 12 year olds who already have a certain jaded, realistic view of the world. So there's kind of this dual arc of the play where Marcel is learning to validate their legitimate fears, while the children are learning to appreciate how Marcel’s antics, frustrating as they sometimes were, saved them from the brink of despair. In the title role, Ethan Slater is able to blend his more traditional acting skills with the clown-like energy of SpongeBob SquarePants. And he's very charming up to a point. Like, there's a fine line between making your character impishly exasperating *for the other characters* Vs. making them genuinely kind of annoying for the audience. I think both the play and the performance sometimes inch a little too close to, or over that line. That, combined with the sometimes repetitive, sometimes a little bit aimless structure, maybe prevented the play from soaring the way it could have with a bit more tightly focused scene work. But for me, they more than made up for that, not just with the story, but also this stylistic vision for the show. Marshall Pailet is the director and co-writer with Ethan Slater, and he uses a lot of little theatrical devices, some pulled from the world of clowning or miming, others just little theatrical flourishes in the use of space and design that really elevated the storytelling. And like I said, the story does have a lot of emotional heft, even outside of the obviously loaded subject matter. So aside from a few quibbles, I do think it was a pretty effective piece overall. So if you're interested, Marcel on the Train is running through March 22nd at Classic Stage Company.
